examples.solution_text:
The left and right halves are mirror images. Both tails fall away equally from the central peak.

The distribution is **symmetrical**.

Curve $A$ has a longer tail to the right, so it is positively skewed. Curve $B$ has mirrored halves, so it is symmetrical.

Curve $C$ has a longer tail to the left, so **curve $C$ is negatively skewed**.

Most marks are low, so the bulk of the data sits on the left. The few high marks form a tail to the right.

The distribution is positively skewed, shown by **curve $B$**.

examples.question_text:
Describe the shape of the distribution of retirement ages.

| Retirement age (years) | Frequency |
| --- | --- |
| 35–39 | 1 |
| 40–44 | 2 |
| 45–49 | 4 |
| 50–54 | 8 |
| 55–59 | 15 |
| 60–64 | 24 |
| 65–69 | 12 |
examples.solution_text:
The largest frequency is $24$, in the $60$–$64$ age group. The frequencies taper off through $15,8,4,2,1$ across five groups to the left, with only one group to the right.

The tail stretches to the left, so the distribution is **negatively skewed**.

**a.** There are two separated peaks, at $25$ and $55$, with a dip between them. The heights $2,10,4,4,10,2$ read the same forwards and backwards, so the whole display has mirrored halves.

The distribution is **bimodal and symmetrical**.

**b.** Every column has frequency $6$, so there is no distinct peak. The two halves are mirror images.

The distribution is **uniform and symmetrical**.

examples.derivation: The heights are 4,11,8,5,2,1. The peak is at 20, followed by four decreasing columns to the right and only one column to the left. The longer right tail supports positive skew, consistent with source Foundation Q2c. The solution diagram preserves the givens and adds the correct tail annotation.

Scores 1–8 have frequencies 1,1,2,3,5,8,6,2. The peak is at score 6; frequencies taper over five positions towards score 1, compared with two positions towards score 8. This supports negative skew using the dot-stack comparison shown in source Foundation Q1b. The solution annotation correctly points left.

Reflection about x=4 pairs the endpoints at 0.3 and 7.7 and the control points at 1.6 and 6.4, and 2.3 and 5.7. The two curve segments are mirror images with a central peak and equal tails. Symmetrical is correct and follows the supplied symmetrical-curve teaching.

A peaks near its left end and extends farther right. B has reflected endpoints and control points about its central peak. C peaks near its right end and extends farther left. Therefore C is negatively skewed. Matching tail direction to a labelled curve follows source Foundation Q3.

Low marks form the bulk on the left; the few high marks extend the distribution to the right. B has its peak near the left and its longer tail to the right, so B is the appropriate positively skewed curve. This adapts the difficult-examination context in source Development Q5b.

The equal-width age groups have frequencies 1,2,4,8,15,24,12. The largest frequency is 24 at 60–64. Moving left from that group gives 15,8,4,2,1 across five groups; only one group lies to its right. Negative skew is correct and uses the distribution-reading method of source Mastery Q9 without introducing relative-frequency calculations.

Panel a has heights 2,10,4,4,10,2: the complete sequence is mirrored, with two peaks at 25 and 55 separated by lower columns. It is bimodal and symmetrical. Panel b has six equal frequencies of 6, so it is uniform with no distinct peak and mirrored halves. Both conclusions follow the supplied modality and symmetry teaching.
